claim: Temperature has been recognized as a key driver of geographical gradients in taxonomic richness across practically all organismal groups.
source: Starting with the pioneering work of Alexander von Humboldt, who in the 19th century identified temperature as a major environmental driver of plant richness along elevational gradients in the Andes (Humboldt and Bonpland, 2010), temperature has been recognized as a key driver of the geographical gradients in taxonomic richness are seen across practically all organismal groups (Rohde, 1992; Gaston, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Humboldt and Bonpland (2010), Rohde (1992), and Gaston (2000).

claim: Zhou et al., 2016 found that soil microbe richness increased across a continental temperature gradient in North America.
source: For example, while Zhou et al., 2016 found that soil microbe richness increased across a continental temperature gradient in North America, others have found unimodal responses (richness peaking at intermediate temperatures) in soils as well as other environments (Milici et al., 2016; Sharp et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: Some studies have found unimodal responses (richness peaking at intermediate temperatures) in soils and other environments.
source: For example, while Zhou et al., 2016 found that soil microbe richness increased across a continental temperature gradient in North America, others have found unimodal responses (richness peaking at intermediate temperatures) in soils as well as other environments (Milici et al., 2016; Sharp et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Milici et al. (2016), Sharp et al. (2014), and Thompson et al. (2017).

claim: The temperature responses of microbial richness or diversity are 'consistently inconsistent,' with no single pattern in terms of shape or direction dominating.
source: Indeed, as demonstrated in the data synthesis by Hendershot et al., 2017, the temperature responses of microbial richness or diversity are 'consistently inconsistent,' with no single pattern in terms of shape (monotonic or unimodal) or direction (positive or negative) dominating.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hendershot et al., 2017.

claim: The metabolic theory of biodiversity (MTB) predicts monotonic increases in species richness with temperature due to increasing cellular kinetic energy at higher temperatures.
source: The first is the metabolic theory of biodiversity (MTB) (Allen et al., 2002), which predicts monotonic increases in species richness with temperature due to increasing cellular kinetic energy at higher temperatures.
evidence: Supported by citation to Allen et al., 2002.

claim: Arroyo et al., 2022 were able to produce a variety of temperature-diversity responses by including a more complex model of enzyme kinetics allowing for unimodal responses.
source: This work was later extended by Arroyo et al., 2022 who were able to produce a variety of temperature-diversity responses by including a more complex model of enzyme kinetics allowing for unimodal responses.
evidence: Supported by citation to Arroyo et al., 2022.

claim: The MTB relies on three key assumptions: (1) all populations have the same rate of energy use (energy equivalence), (2) identical temperature dependence across taxa (the 'Universal Temperature Dependence' or 'UTD'), and (3) non-interacting populations.
source: The MTB and its newer applications are able to recreate various temperature-diversity patterns but rely on three key assumptions: (1) all populations have the same rate of energy use (energy equivalence), (2) identical temperature dependence across taxa (the 'Universal Temperature Dependence' or 'UTD'), and (3) non-interacting populations.
evidence: Direct statement about the assumptions of MTB.

claim: There is some evidence for energy equivalence in phytoplankton communities.
source: Whilst there is some evidence for the energy equivalence in phytoplankton communities (Ghedini et al., 2020) its validity remains, to the best of our knowledge, untested in heterotrophic microbes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ghedini et al., 2020.

claim: The validity of energy equivalence remains untested in heterotrophic microbes.
source: Whilst there is some evidence for the energy equivalence in phytoplankton communities (Ghedini et al., 2020) its validity remains, to the best of our knowledge, untested in heterotrophic microbes.
evidence: Statement about the lack of testing in heterotrophic microbes.

claim: There is extensive evidence for significant functional variation in thermal sensitivities across the microbial tree of life.
source: Support for the other assumptions is weaker and there is now extensive evidence for significant functional variation in thermal sensitivities across the microbial tree of life (Smith et al., 2019; Dell et al., 2011; Kontopoulos et al., 2020) emphasising the fact that the UTD is at best an approximation (Savage, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al. (2019), Dell et al. (2011), and Kontopoulos et al. (2020).

claim: The Universal Temperature Dependence (UTD) is at best an approximation.
source: Support for the other assumptions is weaker and there is now extensive evidence for significant functional variation in thermal sensitivities across the microbial tree of life (Smith et al., 2019; Dell et al., 2011; Kontopoulos et al., 2020) emphasising the fact that the UTD is at best an approximation (Savage, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Savage (2004) and inference from evidence of variation in thermal sensitivities.

claim: Extensive theoretical and empirical evidence shows that resource-mediated species interactions among microbes are the norm and drive community species dynamics and diversity.
source: Likewise, extensive theoretical and empirical evidence shows that resource-mediated species interactions among microbes are the norm and drive community species dynamics and diversity (Goldford et al., 2018; Marsland et al., 2019; Ratzke et al., 2020; Cook et al., 2021; Lechón et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goldford et al. (2018), Marsland et al. (2019), Ratzke et al. (2020), Cook et al. (2021), and Lechón et al. (2021).

claim: The metabolic niche hypothesis posits that there are more energetically viable ways to make a living at intermediate (non-extreme) temperatures.
source: A second explanation for temperature-diversity gradients is the metabolic niche hypothesis (Sharp et al., 2014) which posits that there are more energetically viable ways to make a living at intermediate (non-extreme) temperatures.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharp et al., 2014.

claim: The metabolic niche hypothesis allows for species coexistence and produces an unimodal temperature-diversity response.
source: This allows for species coexistence and in turn produces an unimodal temperature-diversity response (Clarke and Gaston, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clarke and Gaston (2006).

claim: Marsland et al., 2020 modelled the metabolic niche hypothesis phenomenologically by imposing additional mortality on consumers to represent less-favorable environmental conditions, recovering the expected unimodal patterns of richness.
source: This mechanism was modelled phenomenologically by Marsland et al., 2020 who imposed additional mortality on consumers to represent less-favorable environmental conditions, recovering the expected unimodal patterns of richness.
evidence: Supported by citation to Marsland et al., 2020.

claim: The metabolic niche hypothesis is unable to explain richness-temperature relationships other than unimodal patterns.
source: Overall the metabolic niche hypothesis assumes that the size of the feasible niche space follows a specific pattern over temperature and is thus unable to explain other richness-temperature relationships.
evidence: Logical inference from the stated assumptions of the metabolic niche hypothesis.

claim: The metabolic niche hypothesis is unable to explain how effects arise explicitly from the action of temperature on individual populations and their thermal responses.
source: Likewise, it is unable to explain how these effects arise explicitly from the action of temperature on individual populations and their thermal responses.
evidence: Direct statement about limitations of the metabolic niche hypothesis.

claim: Variation in thermal responses is ubiquitous across microbial taxa.
source: We posit that the variation in thermal responses will in fact be important in determining the responses of microbial community richness to temperature. In addition to its ubiquity (Smith et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2021; Kontopoulos et al., 2020) variations on thermal responses may act in two ways.
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al. (2019), Smith et al. (2021), and Kontopoulos et al. (2020).

claim: Nonlinear thermal responses of metabolic traits mean that inter-specific variation in thermal sensitivity will likely drive significant changes in realised trait-value distributions and species interactions at different temperatures.
source: First, the nonlinear thermal responses of metabolic traits means that inter-specific variation in thermal sensitivity will likely drive significant changes in realised trait-value distributions and species interactions at different temperatures.
evidence: Logical inference from the nonlinear nature of thermal responses.

claim: Differences in thermal responses of traits between interacting populations ('physiological mismatches') may have non-trivial effects on microbial community dynamics and coexistence.
source: Second, differences in thermal responses of traits between interacting populations ('physiological mismatches') may have non-trivial effects on microbial community dynamics and coexistence (Dell et al., 2014; Bestion et al., 2018; García et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dell et al. (2014), Bestion et al. (2018), and García et al. (2023).

claim: Competitive interactions have been shown to have strong effects on coexistence and richness in microbial communities.
source: We focus on competitive interactions which have been shown to have string effects on coexistence and richness in microbial communities (Marsland et al., 2019; Goldford et al., 2018; Ratzke et al., 2020; Lechón et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marsland et al. (2019), Goldford et al. (2018), Ratzke et al. (2020), and Lechón et al. (2021).

claim: Feasibility is a necessary condition for stable population coexistence.
source: Feasibility is a necessary condition for stable population coexistence and generally falls as richness increases, placing an upper bound on community size (Goh and Jennings, 1977; Grilli et al., 2017; Dougoud et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goh and Jennings (1977), Grilli et al. (2017), and Dougoud et al. (2018).

claim: Feasibility generally falls as richness increases, placing an upper bound on community size.
source: Feasibility is a necessary condition for stable population coexistence and generally falls as richness increases, placing an upper bound on community size (Goh and Jennings, 1977; Grilli et al., 2017; Dougoud et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goh and Jennings (1977), Grilli et al. (2017), and Dougoud et al. (2018).

claim: The Boltzmann-Arrhenius equation is a sufficiently accurate model for the temperature dependence of metabolically 'higher-level' traits such as interaction and growth rates.
source: The Boltzmann-Arrhenius equation is a sufficiently accurate model for the temperature dependence of metabolically 'higher-level' traits such as interaction and growth rates, because these ultimately emerge from cellular biochemical kinetics (Gillooly et al., 2001; Savage, 2004; Dell et al., 2011; Dell et al., 2014; Arroyo et al., 2022) (see SEC:Methods).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gillooly et al. (2001), Savage (2004), Dell et al. (2011), Dell et al. (2014), and Arroyo et al. (2022).

claim: The empirical validity of Boltzmann for growth rate (r) is now well-established.
source: The empirical validity of Boltzmann for r is now well-established (Smith et al., 2019; Kontopoulos et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al. (2019) and Kontopoulos et al. (2020).

claim: A Boltzmann-Arrhenius (or at least exponential-like) temperature dependence of interaction strength is likely to be a good description because pairwise microbial competitive interactions are ultimately driven by the two species' resource uptake rates.
source: We posit that a Boltzmann-Arrhenius (or at least exponential-like) temperature dependence of interaction strength is likely to be a good description, however, because pairwise microbial competitive interactions are ultimately driven by the two species' resource uptake rates, as shown by the derivation of effective interaction strengths in more mechanistic consumer-resource models of microbial communities (Marsland et al., 2020).
evidence: Logical inference supported by citation to Marsland et al. (2020).

claim: Uptake rates are known to follow a Boltzmann-Arrhenius form within the OTR.
source: As uptake rates are known to follow a Boltzmann-Arrhenius form within the OTR (Smith et al., 2021; Bestion et al., 2018) it follows that the interaction strength may follow this exponential-like form too.
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al. (2021) and Bestion et al. (2018).

claim: A bivariate normal distribution captures the mean and variance of the thermal dependence of traits across the community, as well as the covariance between them.
source: A bivariate normal distribution captures the mean and variance of the thermal dependence of these traits across the community, as well as the covariance between them.
evidence: Direct statement about the properties of the bivariate normal distribution.

claim: Negative covariance relaxes the bound for unimodal response and reduces the degree of variation needed for a unimodal response.
source: As the covariance is expected to be negative this relaxes the bound, and reduce the degree of variation needed for a unimodal response.
evidence: Logical inference from the mathematical condition.

claim: Mean thermal sensitivity of interactions ⟨a⟩ determines the direction and steepness of the temperature-richness relationship.
source: (A) Mean thermal sensitivity of interactions ⟨a⟩ determines the direction and steepness of the temperature-richness relationship.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A with analytical predictions and numerical simulations.

claim: Increasing variance of thermal sensitivity increases unimodality in the temperature-richness relationship.
source: (B) Increasing variance of thermal sensitivity increases unimodality.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B with analytical predictions and numerical simulations.

claim: The analytical predictions match the simulated results well.
source: Figure 2 shows that the analytical predictions match the simulated results well and that the changes in richness over temperature respond to changes in the thermal physiology parameters as expected.
evidence: Comparison between analytical predictions (solid lines) and numerical simulations (dots) in Figure 2.

claim: The predictions of the theory break down when the assumptions of the mean field approximation are not met, primarily when interactions are strong or their variation is large.
source: In general, we expect this will occur when the assumptions of the mean field approximation are not met, primarily when interactions are strong or their variation is large and the coupling between individual populations dominates dynamics (see SEC:Methods for more detail).
evidence: Logical inference from the assumptions of the mean field approximation.

claim: High average strength of interspecific interactions increases error.
source: Likewise high average strength of interspecific interactions increases error whilst increasing the average strength of intraspecific interactions decreases error.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3 sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Increasing the average strength of intraspecific interactions decreases error.
source: Likewise high average strength of interspecific interactions increases error whilst increasing the average strength of intraspecific interactions decreases error.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3 sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Parameterising the theory with empirical values predicts unimodal temperature-richness responses due to the combination of variance and negative covariance.
source: Parameterising our theory with these values (using the same thermal response for growth rates and interactions) predicts unimodal temperature-richness responses due to this combination of variance and negative covariance Figure 4E.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4E with predictions based on empirical data.

claim: The response based on the experimental data shows a sharper increase in richness and peaks at a higher temperature of ∼20°C than that based on the data-synthesis which peaks at ∼9°C.
source: Due to its larger variance in E as well as stronger negative covariance, the response based on the experimental data shows a sharper increase in richness, and peaks at a higher temperature of ∼20°C, than that based on the data-synthesis which has a shallower, broader temperature-richness curve peaking at ∼9°C.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4E comparing predictions from two datasets.

claim: The unimodal pattern is due to the non-linear temperature dependence of trait variance (Equation 4) and its effects on the community-level traits that determine richness (Equations 5 and 6).
source: This is due to the non-linear temperature dependence of trait variance (Equation 4) and its effects on the community-level traits that determine richness (Equations 5 and 6).
evidence: Logical inference from the mathematical derivations.

claim: The negative covariance case is consistent with a thermal generalist-specialist trade-off seen in existing data.
source: This negative covariance case is consistent with a thermal generalist-specialist trade-off seen in existing data analysed here; Smith et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2021 and suggests richness should peak towards the higher end of the operational temperature ranges (OTRs) of most mesophilic bacteria.
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al. (2019) and Smith et al. (2021) and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mechanism presented provides an alternate explanation for the existence of temperature diversity patterns based on ecological processes (i.e. competition).
source: The mechanism we present here provides an alternate explanation for the existence of temperature diversity patterns and is based on ecological processes (i.e. competition).
evidence: Direct statement about the nature of the mechanism.

claim: The model is able to produce richness peaks below the thermal optima of the underlying rates unlike previous explanations which assume declines in richness happen due to a reduction in performance at the population level.
source: Furthermore, our model is able to produce richness peaks below the thermal optima of the underlying rates unlike the previous explanations which assume declines in richness happen due to a reduction in performance at the population level.
evidence: Comparison with previous theories and inference from the model results.

claim: The peak of richness below the thermal optima of individual population rates is consistent with observations of unimodal temperature-richness relationships which tend to be below estimates of microbial thermal optima.
source: This peak of richness below the thermal optima of individual population rates is consistent with observations of unimodal temperature-richness relationships (Milici et al., 2016; Sharp et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2017) which tend to be below estimates of microbial thermal optima (Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Milici et al. (2016), Sharp et al. (2014), Thompson et al. (2017), and Smith et al. (2019).

claim: The mechanisms proposed are not mutually exclusive with previous explanations and patterns of diversity observed in nature are likely the product of multiple processes acting in unison.
source: Crucially we would like to stress that these mechanisms are not mutually exclusive and that the patterns of diversity observed in nature are likely the product of multiple processes acting in unison.
evidence: Speculation about the nature of ecological processes.

claim: The proposed mechanism will be particularly relevant in communities where system dynamics are driven primarily by species interactions.
source: Overall we expect that the mechanism we propose here will be particularly relevant to predicting the temperature-richness relationship in: (i) communities where system dynamics are driven primarily by species interactions (as opposed to scenarios where dynamic assembly and processes such as environmental filtering or neutral processes dominate);
evidence: Speculation about the applicability of the mechanism.

claim: The proposed mechanism will be particularly relevant in environments where species typically experience temperatures within their OTR.
source: (ii) environments where species typically experience temperatures within their OTR (arguably the most common scenario on planet Earth);
evidence: Speculation about the applicability of the mechanism.

claim: The proposed mechanism will be particularly relevant at scales where trait TPC distributions are relatively constant across communities and thus independent of the local environment.
source: (iii) At scales where trait TPC distributions are relatively constant across communities and thus independent of the local environment.
evidence: Speculation about the applicability of the mechanism.

claim: At larger scales, processes such as local adaptation are likely to alter TPC distributions as organisms adapt to local temperature regimes.
source: At larger scales, we expect that processes such as local adaptation are likely to alter these distributions (Kontopoulos et al., 2018) as organisms adapt to local temperature regimes.
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to Kontopoulos et al. (2018).

claim: The constriction of growth rate variation at ∼23°C in the experimental data results in a higher predicted peak of species richness at ∼23°C.
source: This drives a constriction of growth rate variation at ∼23°C in the experimental data, which in turn results in a higher predicted peak of species richness at ∼23°C these data.
evidence: Inference from the data analysis and model predictions.

claim: The temperature at which the growth rate variation constricts in the lab dataset is almost identical to the temperature at which those strains were maintained, suggesting a role of species sorting, acclimation or evolution.
source: In particular, the temperature at which the growth rate variation constricts in the lab dataset is almost identical to the temperature at which those strains were maintained, suggesting a role of species sorting, acclimation or evolution.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed pattern in the data.

claim: The predicted ∼9°C peak in species richness based on the literature-synthesised data is almost identical to that observed by Thompson et al., 2017 from a wide range of environmental samples.
source: Interestingly, the predicted ∼9°C peak in species richness based on these data is almost identical to that observed by Thompson et al., 2017 from a wide range of environmental samples, which also presumably emerges from a heterogeneous set of taxa.
evidence: Comparison with empirical observations from Thompson et al. (2017).

claim: Feasibility is an important limit as only feasible fixed points allow the coexistence of populations within the community.
source: We argue that feasibility is an important limit as only feasible fixed points allow the coexistence of populations within the community.
evidence: Logical inference from the definition of feasibility.

claim: Goh and Jennings, 1977 showed the scaling of system size with feasibility in GLV communities based on random parameterisations.
source: Feasibility has long been discussed in the literature in this way, going back to Goh and Jennings, 1977 who showed the scaling of system size with feasibility in GLV communities based on random parameterisations.
evidence: Supported by citation to Goh and Jennings (1977).

claim: Feasible fixed points in the GLV are almost always stable.
source: In this context, it is worth noting that feasible fixed points in the GLV are almost always stable (Gibbs et al., 2018), suggesting that patterns of stability-constrained richness should follow the same temperature response.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gibbs et al. (2018).

claim: The GLV underlying the theory assumes a physically well-mixed system where spatial structure does not play a role.
source: We also note that the GLV underlying our theory assumes a physically well-mixed system, that is, the spatial structure does not play a role.
evidence: Direct statement about the assumptions of the model.

claim: Spatial structure will impact species coexistence, for instance, by localising competitive exclusion to spatial 'pockets.'
source: As such, spatial structure will impact species coexistence, for instance, by localising competitive exclusion to spatial 'pockets.'
evidence: Speculation about the effects of spatial structure.

claim: It has been argued that competitive interactions dominate in microbial communities.
source: Whilst it has been argued that competitive interactions dominate in microbial communities (Foster and Bell, 2012) there has more recently been a recognition of the importance of cooperative interactions that develop through cross-feeding between strains on their metabolic-by-products (Goldford et al., 2018; Marsland et al., 2019; Lechón et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Foster and Bell (2012), Goldford et al. (2018), Marsland et al. (2019), and Lechón et al. (2021).

claim: There has been a recognition of the importance of cooperative interactions that develop through cross-feeding between strains on their metabolic-by-products.
source: Whilst it has been argued that competitive interactions dominate in microbial communities (Foster and Bell, 2012) there has more recently been a recognition of the importance of cooperative interactions that develop through cross-feeding between strains on their metabolic-by-products (Goldford et al., 2018; Marsland et al., 2019; Lechón et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goldford et al. (2018), Marsland et al. (2019), and Lechón et al. (2021).

claim: The approach towards determining the temperature dependence of trait distributions could be applied to other models such as microbial consumer-resource models.
source: Our approach towards determining the temperature dependence of trait distributions could, however, be applied to other models such as the recently-introduced microbial consumer-resource models (Marsland et al., 2019), which would allow explicit characterisation of resource-mediated interactions and thus the higher-order interactions and indirect effects that arise.
evidence: Speculation about future applications supported by citation to Marsland et al. (2019).

claim: The broad effects of distributions of thermal response parameters are expected to have similar effects in consumer-resource models though the exact mapping of trait distributions on to richness may change.
source: We do not use this class of models here due to the additional complexity resource dynamics add and the existence of many analytical techniques to study the GLV. However, we would still expect the broad effects of distributions of thermal response parameters to have similar effects (as the thermal responses of traits are independent of the system dynamics) though the exact mapping of trait distributions (and the traits that need to be considered) on to richness may change.
evidence: Speculation about the generality of the results.

claim: The temperature-richness relationship in microbial communities can be strongly driven by variations in thermal physiology across species.
source: Overall, our results provide a compelling theoretical basis and empirical evidence that the temperature-richness relationship in microbial communities can be strongly driven by variations in thermal physiology across species.
evidence: Summary statement based on the theoretical and empirical results presented.

claim: Quantifying variation in thermal physiology in local communities is likely to be key to predicting the effects of temperature fluctuations on microbial community diversity across space and time.
source: Whilst often ignored, quantifying this variation in local communities are likely to be key to predicting the effects of temperature fluctuations on microbial community diversity across space and time.
evidence: Speculation about the importance of quantifying variation.

claim: The mean-field approximation assumes that the community is large such that interactions can be considered in terms of their average value and the effect of any individual interaction is small.
source: This approximation assumes that the community we consider is large such that interactions can be considered in terms of their average value and the effect of any individual interaction is small.
evidence: Direct statement about the assumptions of the mean-field approximation.

claim: The mean-field approximation assumes that the covariance term is negligible, which is equivalent to saying that any individual interaction between the focal species and another species' population has a small effect on its biomass abundance.
source: It also assumes that the second covariance term is negligible, which is equivalent to saying that any individual interaction between the focal species and another species' population has a small effect on its biomass abundance.
evidence: Direct statement about the assumptions of the mean-field approximation.

claim: The covariance term will be small as long as the correlation and the variation in interaction strengths are small.
source: Thus, the covariance term will be small as long as the correlation and the variation in interaction strengths are small.
evidence: Logical inference from the decomposition of covariance.

claim: The thermal optima of growth rates of mesophilic prokaryotes in laboratory experiments are typically 5–10°C higher than their (constant) ambient temperature.
source: Indeed, the thermal optima of growth rates of mesophilic prokaryotes in laboratory experiments are typically 5–10°C higher than their (constant) ambient temperature Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al. (2019).

claim: E distributions tend to be right-skewed.
source: On the other hand, E distributions tend to be right-skewed (Kontopoulos et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2019; Dell et al., 2011), but we use the normal distribution here as an adequate approximation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kontopoulos et al. (2020), Smith et al. (2019), and Dell et al. (2011).
